questions.stem: A 57-year-old man was brought into the Emergency Department in a state of collapse. He was known to have end-stage liver disease. He had been bitten on the calf by a neighbor’s dog 5 days beforehand. He had not sought medical care immediately following the injury. On examination, he was profoundly unwell. His temperature was 35.2°C, blood pressure 72/42 mmHg, heart rate 142 beats/min, GCS 14/15. There were multiple purpuric lesions over his torso and limbs. The bite injury was scabbed but clean, with no pus or erythema. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 30 mL/min Lactate 4.6 mmol/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Capnocytophaga canimorsus Capnocytophaga canimorsus, commonly found in canine oral flora, can cause bacteremia and fulminant sepsis in humans, particularly those with asplenia or underlying liver disease. All of the organisms may be involved in bite injury infections, whether human, dog, or cat bite.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q28

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman was bitten by a Rhesus macaque on the forearm. The wound was thoroughly irrigated after the injury, and she was started on amoxicillin/clavulanate.
questions.lead_in: What other prophylactic agent should she be offered?
questions.explanation: Aciclovir Monkey bites involving macaques carry the risk for transmission of B virus, a herpesvirus that can cause fatal encephalomyelitis in humans. Postexposure prophylaxis with either aciclovir or valaciclovir is appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q28

questions.question: You are called about a man attacked by a dog.

parts.text: What interventions would you recommend right now?

cohort_answer.text: Local wound care (cleansing with soap/water and antiseptic, remove foreign bodies, do not suture closed); consider antimicrobial prophylaxis (Clavulin x3-5 days) if high risk area/close to bone-joint/vascular-lymphatic insufficiency/deep puncture or crush injury; surgical consult if evidence of infection; asplenic patients always get prophylaxis; tetanus prophylaxis; risk assessment for rabies (dog's vaccination status, wild/domestic, local prevalence); quarantine dog 10 days and observe; if high risk (rabid dog) consider Rabies Ig 20 IU/kg + rabies vaccine (4 doses 0,3,7,14); report to public health

questions.question: You see a 6 year-old child presenting following a cat bite, who he was playing “aggressively” with. On examination, there are 2 puncture wounds on the left arm, with no surrounding erythema or edema

parts.text: Presuming no antibiotic allergies, what antibiotic should be given for prophylaxis?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has not received any immunizations after 4 months?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he is HIV positive has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?

questions.model_answer:
a) Prophylactic antibiotic: amoxicillin-clavulanate (covers Pasteurella multocida as well as oral anaerobes/streptococci from the cat's mouth).
b) Fully immunized except for pre-school boosters (tetanus-prone puncture wound): give a Tdap (or Td) booster now, as the primary series is complete but the age-appropriate booster is overdue; tetanus immune globulin (TIG) is not needed since the primary series was completed.
c) No immunizations after 4 months of age (incomplete primary series, tetanus-prone wound): give both the age-appropriate tetanus-containing vaccine (to complete/continue the primary series) AND tetanus immune globulin (TIG), since the primary series is incomplete.
d) HIV-positive, immunized except pre-school boosters (tetanus-prone wound): give the Tdap (or Td) booster AND tetanus immune globulin (TIG) - immunocompromised patients should receive TIG for tetanus-prone wounds regardless of vaccination history, as their immune response to prior vaccination may be inadequate.
questions.beyond_mandell: ACIP/Canadian Immunization Guide tetanus prophylaxis wound management recommendations, including the immunocompromised host modification.

questions.question: 6yo child presents after a cat bite from playing too aggressively with family cat. Bite is two puncture marks on the arm, is clean with no surrounding erythema.

parts.text: If no drug allergies, what is the preferred prophylactic antibiotic? (0.5)
If the childhood immunizations were up to date except for pre-school boosters. What would you do with regards to tetanus (0.5)
If the child had only received vaccines up to and including 4 months old - what do you do for tetanus in this situation (1)
If the child was HIV+ and immunizations and was UTD except for pre-school boosters, what do you do for tetanus (1)

cohort_answer.text: Antibiotic: Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (second line TMP/SMX or ceftriaxone + clindamycin, Redbook). Indications for prophylaxis: Immunocompromised; Cat bites; Puncture wounds; Hand, foot or genital involvement; Moderate or severe wounds especially with baseline edema/crush injury; Deep or surgically closed facial wounds. TIG only given if not received 3 dose series previously, or has humoral immune deficiency regardless of immunization status (including heme malignancies and HIV) if wound not minor/clean. Pre-school boosters missing: Give booster as due, no TIG. Only vaccinated to 4 months (2 doses): Need to vaccinate (restart series) and give TIG; can do accelerated course (4 weeks between doses 1,2,3 and 6-12 months between dose 3-4 and 4-5; dose 5 not needed if child over 4 years, so 3 doses 4 weeks apart then 4th booster 6 months later). HIV+ with pre-school boosters missing: Give booster dose and TIG. 'Individuals with humoral immune deficiency who have wounds that are not minor and clean should receive both TIG and tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine, regardless of the time elapsed since the last booster'
